entries.english:
Co-plaintiffs/applicants/interveners: Ludger von Mansbach on behalf of his wife Margarethe von Eberstein; Quirin von Carben on behalf of his wife Katharina von Eberstein, widow of Philipp von Karsbach; and Kunigunde von Eberstein, widow of Oswald von Fechenbach, as heirs of the brothers Philipp and Mangold von Eberstein (Ludger von Mansbach, Philipp von Karsbach, and Oswald von Fechenbach were plaintiffs and counter-defendants at first instance).
Co-defendant/intervener: Prince-Abbot Wolfgang I of Fulda (Prince-Abbot Philipp of Fulda was defendant and counter-plaintiff at first instance), and Hartmann von Boineburg, Fulda's princely bailiff at Fürsteneck, Martin von Haun, Eberhard and Christoph von der Tann, appointed as arbitrators.
Counsel for plaintiffs: Dr. Wolfgang Breyning and Dr. Malachias Ramminger (1557); Lic. Jakob Erhardt (1583); Dr. Sigismund Haffner (1600). Counsel for defendant: Dr. Jaspar Fichardt (1554); Dr. Ludwig Stahel (1569); Dr. Bernhard Küehorn (1584).
Contemporary subject: appeal or nullity. Modern subject: dispute over various jurisdictions in the Bieberstein district and Hofbieber centena (called Hofbibra in the file).
At first instance: After agreements with Philipp von Eberstein to resolve by arbitration the disputes concerning Bieberstein district and Hofbieber centena, Prince-Abbot Philipp agreed with the Eberstein heirs to an arbitral proceeding under the customary rules for disputes between the prince-bishopric and the knighthood. He sued the heirs for: (1) repeated attempts to exempt their subjects from Hofbieber centena court by forbidding them to attend the Pentecost court day, which all residents of the district had to attend without summons, to deliver centena oats and the free messenger's loaf, and to perform labor services; (2) claims for rent on clearings made without authorization on Fulda land; (3) unauthorized wine sales at Schackau (called Schacken in the file); and (4) claims to possession and rents in the territories of Schwarzbach, Bernhards below the Milseburg, Grabenhauck, and a field between Findlos (called Fundlos in the file) and Wickers; rights to timber in a woodland between Dörmbach and Steens and at Quernberg, Schweinsberg, and Bomberg; and sheep and livestock grazing on a field between Liebhards (called Lieberts in the file) and Eckweisbach, claimed by Philipp and Mangold von Eberstein, their heirs, and their subjects, rent-payers, and fief-holders at Langenberg, Eckweisbach, Rupsroth, and Wickers.
The heirs counterclaimed for: (1) seizure of parts of the Langenwinden woodland, the castle estate at Bieberstein, and Stephanswiese, all Fulda fiefs held by the Eberstein family; (2) damage to the Eberstein mills at Langenbieber (called Langenbibra in the file), Kleinsassen (called Sachsen), Ödensten, Schackau, and Weihers below Bieberstein caused by newly built mills; and (3) the forced subjection of the shepherdies at Schackau and Eckweisbach to homage.
The plaintiffs' heirs challenged as null the April 1556 judgment based on an opinion of Heidelberg University's law faculty. The arbitrators ordered it enforced. The heirs appealed to the Imperial Chamber Court, alleging that the arbitrators had omitted the required attempt at amicable settlement, failed to decide all claims while deciding matters outside them, and merely read—but did not formally pronounce—the law faculty's opinion.
On 26 June 1577, while retaining several provisions of the first-instance judgment, the Imperial Chamber Court required the plaintiffs' subjects to attend the Pentecost court day, provide centena oats, the free messenger's loaf, and labor services, and render homage to the prince-abbot as territorial lord as well as to the heirs as rent-lords. It rejected the plaintiffs' claim to exemption from customs duties, confirmed their right to levy taxes, ordered restoration of the Bieber's former course, allowed the Fulda mill at Weihers to continue operating, and delimited the disputed territories. Further disputes arose during boundary marking by an imperial commission (see order no. 4961). The abbey obtained enforcement orders on 25 January 1580, 23 September 1597, and 19 August 1598; the plaintiffs' party obtained one on 30 March 1598.
Instances: (1) Hartmann von Boineburg, Martin von Haun, Eberhard and Christoph von der Tann, appointed arbitrators; (2) Imperial Chamber Court, 1557–1601.
The incomplete preliminary file contains Fulda's exhibits: extracts from privileges of Charlemagne for Abbot Sturmi (774), Louis the Pious for Abbot Ratgar (816), Otto II (980), and undated privileges of emperors Louis IV and Charles IV; witness statements before Fulda's Bieberstein office (1496); fief reversals by Philipp von Eberstein (1515) and his heirs (1546) for Fulda fiefs at Schackau, Kleinsassen, Langenbieber, Langenberg, Bieberstein, Eckweisbach, Herölds, Weiperz (called Weiprechts), Brückenau, and elsewhere; and Abbot Johann III's fief charter to Paul Dietrich for deserted settlements at Ober- and Unterhauck (1506). An execution commission report includes an inspection record (1573); another includes inspection and boundary-stone records by land surveyors (1578–1579) and Wilhelm Besserer of Speyer's oath. Fulda chancery protocols concern negotiations over homage by the plaintiffs' rent-payers (1597), with a report by Hofbieber's centgraf. Also included are a fief reversal (1598) by Karl, Georg Friedrich, and Friedrich Geuß von Mansbach, Quirin Riedesel von Bellersheim, Adam Hektor von Rosenbach, Daniel Adam, Hans Reichard, and Hans Karl von Fechenbach; the defendants' costs and supporting records; a 1421 purchase contract between Prince-Abbot Johann I of Fulda and Eberhard von Eberstein for property at Kleinsassen; receipts for the plaintiffs' Turkish tax payments (1598); invitations to Eberstein heirs to attend Franconian knightly assemblies (1558–1589), and Emperor Maximilian II's mandate to numerous members of the Rhön-Werra knightly canton to attend the 1575 assembly; extracts from Fulda tax registers (1547–1598); petitions by the pastors of Eckweisbach and Hofbieber to Fulda's governor concerning the former's presentation by the plaintiffs (1597–1598), and a list of the latter's lost income; reports on pilgrimage to the (St. Gangolf) chapel on the Milseburg and the opening of Kleinsassen church by Hofbieber's centgraf (1598); and Imperial Chamber Court mandates in the Eberstein heirs' case against Fulda's government concerning a censure proceeding at Hofbieber centena court and the arrest of Eberstein subjects at Dietges (1583, 1584).
File notes: process began 1557. Prior instances: Boineburg family (baronial/countly, arbitrators); Haun family (arbitrators); Heidelberg; von der Tann family (arbitrators).
